chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Angel Investing Really Is

lessons.title: The Indian Angel Ecosystem: Networks, Syndicates and Platforms

children.text: In the first lesson, the deal came to you because Arjun happened to be your college friend. That is luck, not a strategy. Most people who want to invest in startups hit the same wall: they have the money but no founders calling them, no way to tell a good pitch from a polished one, and no idea what fair terms look like. India has built an entire ecosystem to solve that problem: angel networks, syndicates, online platforms and SEBI-registered angel funds. This lesson shows how each one works, what it costs you, and which doors are actually open to you under SEBI's current rules.

body.text: A new angel's scarcest resource is not money. It is access to good deals and the judgement to pick among them. Networks, syndicates and platforms sell you both, and every one of them charges for it in fees, carry or control.

children.text: Four Routes Into a Startup Deal

cells: You meet a founder, agree terms and receive shares in your own name
Friends, former colleagues, founder introductions on LinkedIn
A members' club screens startups and hosts pitch meetings; members decide deal by deal
A screening team plus experienced members who lead deals
Indian Angel Network, Mumbai Angels, Chennai Angels, Hyderabad Angels
A lead investor brings a deal and other investors co-invest behind them, usually online
LetsVenture, AngelList India, Inflection Point Ventures
A pooled vehicle registered as a Category I AIF invests in startups on behalf of its investors
Funds set up by networks and platforms, searchable on SEBI's AIF list

body.text: The lines between these routes blur in practice. Many networks and platforms run their own syndicates and also operate SEBI-registered angel funds, so one brand may offer you two or three routes. Always ask one precise question: in this deal, will the shares sit in my name, or will I own units of a fund that holds the shares?

children.text: Angel Networks: Investing as a Club

Organised angel investing in India began in 2006, when both the Indian Angel Network in Delhi and Mumbai Angels were founded. Today, Tracxn tracks around 160 angel networks in India, from national groups to city-focused ones in Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune and Kolkata. A network does not usually invest its own money. It filters startups, organises pitches and paperwork, and lets members decide individually whether to put money in.
A typical network deal moves through five stages:
Application.
Founders submit a pitch deck and basic financials.
Screening.
The network's team and a few members shortlist the most promising companies.
Pitch meeting.
Shortlisted founders present to members, who ask questions and signal interest.
Due diligence and term sheet.
One or two experienced members check the business, the numbers and the legal records, and negotiate valuation and terms.
Commitment and closing.
Interested members commit amounts, documents are signed and money is transferred.

body.title: How selective is the funnel?
body.prompt: In the illustrative funnel above, 3 of 1,000 applicants get funded. What percentage of applicants is that?
body.explanation: 3 ÷ 1,000 = 0.003, or 0.3%. This filtering is the real value of a network. A solo angel who meets 10 founders a year and funds 3 of them is being about 100 times less selective.

children.text: Syndicates: Following a Lead Investor

markDefs.definition: The experienced investor who finds a deal, negotiates the terms, invests their own money and manages the relationship with the founder on behalf of everyone in the syndicate.
A share of the profits paid to the lead investor or platform, taken only if the investment makes money.

children.text: A syndicate is a group of investors who back a startup together behind one
lead investor
. The lead does the sourcing and homework, and the backers write smaller cheques alongside. In return, the lead usually earns
carry

on the backers' profits, and the platform may charge its own fees. LetsVenture was founded in 2013 and launched lead syndicates in 2016. AngelList brought its syndicates model to India in January 2018.

body.caption: Example: you invest ₹5 lakh, your stake returns ₹50 lakh and total carry is 20%. Carry = 20% × ₹45 lakh profit = ₹9 lakh, so you receive ₹41 lakh.

body.title: What carry costs you
body.prompt: You invest ₹10 lakh through a syndicate. At exit, your stake is worth ₹40 lakh. The lead and platform together take 15% carry on profits. How much do you receive, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: Profit = ₹40 lakh − ₹10 lakh = ₹30 lakh. Carry = 15% × ₹30 lakh = ₹4.5 lakh. You receive ₹40 lakh − ₹4.5 lakh = ₹35.5 lakh. If the startup fails, there is no profit and no carry, but any upfront fees you paid are still gone.

body.title: Investing alone vs through a syndicate

columns.label: Investing alone
points: You choose every deal and negotiate your own terms
Deal flow limited to the founders you personally know
All diligence, legal checks and follow-ups are your job

columns.label: Through a syndicate
points: Access to deals you would never see on your own
An experienced lead does most of the diligence
Smaller cheques make it easier to spread money across many startups
Carry and fees reduce your returns, and you rely on the lead's judgement

children.text: SEBI Angel Funds and the Accredited Investor Rule

markDefs.definition: An investor certified by a SEBI-recognised accreditation agency as meeting minimum income or net worth thresholds, which allows access to certain products with lighter regulatory protection.

children.text: An angel fund is a sub-category of venture capital fund within Category I AIFs. SEBI overhauled the rules in September 2025. Angel funds registered after 10 September 2025 can offer deals only to
accredited investors

, and must onboard at least five of them before their first close. The old ₹25 lakh minimum commitment per investor was removed, and a fund can now invest between ₹10 lakh and ₹25 crore in any single startup. Older angel funds could not take fresh money from non-accredited investors after 8 September 2026, and must be fully compliant by 31 March 2027.

body.caption: Accredited investor thresholds for individuals, HUFs and family trusts (meet any one)

body.title: Is Meera accredited?
body.question: Meera, a Hyderabad cardiologist, earns ₹1.4 crore a year and has a net worth of ₹4 crore, of which ₹2.2 crore is in mutual funds and shares. Does she qualify as an accredited investor?
options: Yes, under Option 1, because her income is above ₹1 crore
Yes, under Option 3, because her income is above ₹1 crore
No, because she fails all three options
Yes, because doctors are automatically accredited
body.explanation: Option 1 needs ₹2 crore of income; she has ₹1.4 crore. Option 2 needs ₹7.5 crore of net worth; she has ₹4 crore. Option 3 needs ₹1 crore of income and ₹5 crore of net worth; her net worth falls short. She cannot invest through angel funds that are restricted to accredited investors.

body.label: Angel fund investment per startup
body.context: Under SEBI's September 2025 amendments, replacing the earlier range of ₹25 lakh to ₹10 crore.

body.text: Accreditation is a wealth test, not a skill test. A ₹2 crore salary does not make anyone better at judging a seed-stage founder. It only signals that SEBI believes you can absorb a loss. The accredited investor rule applies to angel funds; buying shares directly in a private company follows company law instead, where a private placement offer can be made to at most 200 people in a financial year, with some exclusions.

children.text: What Each Route Costs You

body.caption: Common cost structures (actual fees vary widely; always read the documents)

cells: Legal and documentation costs, if any
Your time, and mistakes from doing diligence alone
Annual membership fee; sometimes a per-deal fee
Sometimes a success fee or carry
Deals are shared with many members, so allocations can be small
Carry to the lead and platform, commonly 10 to 20% of profits
You depend on the lead's judgement and incentives
Money moves only when the fund manager decides

body.text: Watch for "startup investing communities" on Instagram, Telegram or WhatsApp that charge a subscription for "exclusive pre-IPO and startup deals" or collect money into someone's bank account to invest on your behalf. Pooling money from many investors without SEBI registration is not a syndicate. If a platform says your money goes into an angel fund or AIF, search for that exact fund name on SEBI's list before you transfer a rupee.

body.label: SEBI: Registered Alternative Investment Funds
body.description: Verify that any angel fund or AIF a platform mentions is actually registered with SEBI.

body.title: Pick Karthik's route
body.scenario: Karthik is a 41-year-old engineering manager in Chennai. He earns ₹60 lakh a year, has a net worth of ₹3 crore, and wants to put ₹15 lakh into startups over the next three years. He has never invested in a startup and works long hours.
body.prompt: Which routes are realistically open to Karthik, and how should he approach them?
body.modelAnswer:
1. He is not an accredited investor. His income is below ₹1 crore and his net worth is below ₹5 crore, so he fails all three options. Angel funds restricted to accredited investors are closed to him.
2. Direct investing is legally open, but it demands time and skill he does not have. It suits him only for a founder he knows very well, and even then with a small cheque.
3. An angel network or syndicate is the most practical route, provided it lets non-accredited investors invest directly in a startup's shares rather than only through an angel fund. He should ask each platform exactly how its deals are structured before signing up.
4. He should spread the ₹15 lakh across several deals over three years instead of two or three large cheques, subject to each platform's minimums.
5. Before following any lead, he should check that lead's past deals and exits, how much of their own money is going in, and the total fees and carry he will pay.

body.title: Name the role
body.textWithBlank: In a syndicate, the experienced investor who finds the deal, negotiates the terms and earns carry is called the ___ investor.
body.explanation: The lead investor sources the deal, does most of the diligence and represents the syndicate with the founder. Carry on the backers' profits is their reward for that work.

cards.definition: A members' club that screens startups and hosts pitches; members decide individually whether to invest.
A group of investors who back a startup together behind one lead investor.
The experienced investor who sources and negotiates a syndicate deal, invests their own money and earns carry.
A share of profits paid to a lead or manager, commonly 10 to 20% in syndicates, charged only if the investment makes money.
A SEBI-registered Category I AIF sub-category that pools money to invest ₹10 lakh to ₹25 crore per startup.
An investor certified as meeting SEBI's income or net worth thresholds, such as ₹2 crore of annual income or ₹7.5 crore of net worth.

points: Indian angels access deals four ways: directly, through angel networks, through syndicates and platforms, or through SEBI-registered angel funds.
Networks filter hundreds of startups down to a handful, which is their core value to a new angel.
Syndicates let you invest behind an experienced lead, who is paid through carry on your profits.
Since September 2025, new SEBI angel funds accept only accredited investors and invest ₹10 lakh to ₹25 crore per startup.
Accreditation needs ₹2 crore of income, ₹7.5 crore of net worth, or ₹1 crore of income plus ₹5 crore of net worth; it is a wealth test, not a skill test.
Always ask how a deal is structured and what it costs in total, and verify any angel fund on SEBI's registered list.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or an endorsement of any network, platform or fund named here. Regulations, fees and eligibility rules change, so check the latest SEBI circulars and each platform's documents. Meera, Karthik and the funnel figures are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
